reason: The dominant geometric feature to compare is whether the hydroxyl O-H group is oriented so that the hydrogen can be acceptor-bound at/near nitrogen, i.e. a short H...N contact with O...N still in a favorable range. I treated the hydroxyl hydrogen as the H in the C-O-H block that is closest to O, then used H...N and O...N distances as a proxy for intramolecular hydrogen-bond strength. I also checked for close nonbonded heavy-atom contacts, especially between the N-ethyl group (N-CH2/CH3) and the CH2OH-bearing carbon, and between the propyl alpha carbon and the CH2OH carbon. Conformer families with H...N roughly 2.2–2.36 A and O...N roughly 2.7–2.85 A are ranked first: 5, 14, 12, 10, 29, 7, 15, 16, 18, 23, 6, 30, 22, 9. Within this group, shorter H...N and similarly favorable O...N are preferred; 5 has the shortest H...N (~2.17 A), while 14, 12, and 10 are all near ~2.22 A. 29 follows with ~2.23 A. 7 and 15 have comparable H...N (~2.27 A), and 16, 18, 23, and 6 are slightly farther (~2.29–2.30 A). 30, 22, and 9 have H...N around 2.35–2.36 A and are therefore placed after that tier despite otherwise good O...N distances. The next tier has a weaker but still present O-H...N contact, with H...N around 2.5–2.65 A and O...N around 2.8–3.0 A: 4, 1, 28, 11, 3, 20, 17, 13. Here 4, 1, and 28 have the shortest H...N contacts and no obvious severe steric clash. 11 has a reasonably short H...N contact but a closer propyl-alcohol region (propyl alpha-C to CH2OH carbon around ~2.3 A), so it is held below 28. 3 and 20 are very similar, with weak H bonding and mild steric congestion; 17 and 13 have the longest H...N contacts in this tier and are placed last in the hydrogen-bonded group. The lowest-energy group here is the set with the hydroxyl hydrogen pointed away from nitrogen, giving H...N distances near 3.8–3.9 A and essentially no intramolecular hydrogen bond: 25, 8, 27, 21, 2, 19, 26, 24. These are ranked mainly by sterics: 25, 8, 27, and 21 are relatively open in the N-ethyl/CH2OH/propyl region, while 2 and 19 are slightly more extended. 26 and 24 are least favorable because they show closer contacts between the N-ethyl substituent and the CH2OH-bearing carbon (roughly C-N-ethyl-to-CH2OH carbon around 2.9 A), adding steric pressure without compensating hydrogen-bond stabilization. Overall uncertainty is nontrivial because the conformers are chemically close, hydrogen-bond strength depends strongly on angle not just distance, the coordinates are not QM-refined, and steric terms for subtle rotamers can partially compensate for a weaker H bond. The final order therefore emphasizes the clear H...N/O...N trend first, then steric crowding, with the weak-hydrogen-bond and no-hydrogen-bond ends expected to be the least certain.

reason: I treated the structures as conformers of the same flexible CH3-CH(CHO)-CH2-O-CH=NH-like chain. The imine C-N distance is consistently short, about 1.25 A, so the terminal fragment is better viewed as an O-CH=NH-type imine ether rather than a freely rotating amine. I first checked for possible N-H donor hydrogen bonds to the carbonyl oxygen and ether oxygen. The closest N-H...O distances are only about 2.8-3.2 A, and in the closest cases the N-H vector is not well aligned with the oxygen acceptor, so there is no strong linear intramolecular hydrogen bond providing a large stabilizing term. Because of this, the ranking is dominated by steric crowding, gauche/eclipsing preferences, and dipole alignment rather than by a single dominant H bond. I therefore compared nonbonded contacts that change between conformers, especially C_imine-to-alpha-carbon distance, N-to-alpha-carbon distance, methyl-to-carbonyl-oxygen distance, methyl-to-ether-oxygen distance, and folded ether-oxygen-to-carbonyl-carbon contacts. More stable conformers are those in which the CH=NH fragment and ether are not folded back too close to the alpha carbon and methyl group, and where no pair of atoms is significantly closer than van der Waals preference would allow. Conformers 12, 13, 25, 6, 11, 27, 8, and 14 are relatively extended and have few close nonbonded contacts, so they are placed near the top even though the exact order among them depends on subtle torsional and dipole effects that are difficult to resolve by coordinates alone. Conformers with isolated mild contacts, such as methyl near carbonyl oxygen or ether oxygen, or a slightly folded O-ether/carbonyl relationship, are placed in the middle; examples include 2, 29, 7, 26, 10, 21, 19, 28, 30, 16, 18, 20, 5, 9, 22, 23, 1, and 17. Structures with a clearly crowded alpha center plus the imine fragment, especially short C_imine-to-alpha-carbon and N-to-alpha-carbon distances, are ranked lower; 15 and 4 are the most crowded of the set, while 3 and 24 are intermediate cases with more folded character. I also noted that C-H...N contacts involving the aldehydic H can occur in some folded structures but are weak compared with the steric penalties and do not rescue the most crowded arrangements. The ordering is therefore a geometry-based estimate: the top and bottom groups are more defensible than the fine ordering inside the middle, because many structures differ only by small gauche/anti preferences, methyl rotamers, and dipole alignment effects that are not fully distinguishable without an explicit energy evaluation.

reason: The geometries were treated as conformers of the same hydroxy-bicyclic/propane-linked C8H14O-type skeleton: one cyclopropane bearing an O-H group, a short methylene chain, and a second cyclopropane. I used the O-H hydrogens (final H in most blocks) and ring carbon separations as the main geometric descriptors. There is no strong intramolecular hydrogen-bond acceptor, so stabilization is mainly from avoiding steric clashes, gauche/syn interactions, and close nonbonded H/C contacts. The most important descriptor was the separation of the two cyclopropane rings, especially C2-C6 (ring-attachment distance) and C1-C6/C1-C7/C1-C8 (distance of the hydroxy-bearing ring carbon to the far ring). A smaller group of conformers has C2-C6 near 3.8-4.1 A and C1-C6 near 4.6-5.1 A, so the two rings are well separated and the chain is broadly anti/extended; these are assigned as the most stable. Within that group I ranked by the average of the six inter-ring C-C separations and by keeping the O-H away from the second ring; 24, 10, and 9 are marginally best because their hydroxy-ring carbon is very far from the second ring, while 12 is the lowest of the group partly because the O-H group is closer to the far ring. A second, larger group has C2-C6 around 3.0-3.3 A, meaning one or more chain dihedral states are gauche-like and the two cyclopropane faces are closer. These were ranked lower, using the same inter-ring separation sum and the presence or absence of O-H pointing toward the second ring; conformers 19, 18, 2, 30, 15, 29, 16, 20, 14, and 21 form the middle of this group, while 22 and 23 are somewhat more folded or less well separated. The least favorable structures combine close C1-C6/C2-C6 contacts with O-H hydrogens that sit only roughly 2.5-3.0 A from second-ring carbons, implying unfavorable H...C/H-H contacts and tighter ring crowding; 7, 13, 25, 6, 3, and 5 occupy the bottom. Several entries are close in estimated strain, especially in the middle of the ranking, so the order within some subsets is uncertain and should be viewed as a geometry-based approximation rather than a quantitative energy ordering.
